faqs.question: How much does it cost to enter Luxor Temple?
faqs.answer: Foreign adults pay approximately 500 EGP, with foreign students paying around 250 EGP with valid ID. Egyptian nationals pay a much lower local rate. Prices are periodically revised by the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.

faqs.question: What are Luxor Temple's opening hours?
faqs.answer: Luxor Temple is typically open from around 6:00 am until about 7:00 pm, later than many other sites, since it is one of the most popular temples to visit after dark under floodlights.

faqs.question: Is Luxor Temple better to visit during the day or at night?
faqs.answer: Many visitors and guides consider Luxor Temple one of the best evening visits in Egypt. Floodlighting after sunset dramatically illuminates the columns, statues, and pylon, and daytime heat is no longer a factor.

faqs.question: Who built Luxor Temple?
faqs.answer: Luxor Temple was primarily built by Pharaoh Amenhotep III around 1400 BCE, with major additions later made by Ramesses II, including the entrance pylon, forecourt, and colossal statues.

faqs.question: Why is there a mosque inside Luxor Temple?
faqs.answer: The Abu al-Haggag Mosque was built centuries ago partly atop and within the ancient temple structure, and it remains an active place of worship today, reflecting more than 3,000 years of continuous religious use at the site.

faqs.question: What happened to Luxor Temple's obelisks?
faqs.answer: The temple originally had a pair of matching obelisks at its entrance. One remains in place at Luxor Temple, while the other was gifted to France in 1830 and now stands in the Place de la Concorde in Paris.

faqs.question: What was the Opet Festival?
faqs.answer: The Opet Festival was an annual ancient Egyptian religious celebration in which statues of the Theban triad—Amun, Mut, and Khonsu—were ceremonially carried from Karnak Temple to Luxor Temple, symbolically renewing the pharaoh's divine authority to rule.

faqs.question: How long does it take to visit Luxor Temple?
faqs.answer: Most visitors spend around 1 to 1.5 hours at Luxor Temple, as it is smaller and more compact than Karnak Temple.

faqs.question: Is Luxor Temple connected to Karnak Temple?
faqs.answer: Yes, historically the two temples were linked by the roughly 2.7 km Avenue of Sphinxes, a processional route used during the Opet Festival, portions of which have been excavated and restored for visitors today.

faqs.question: Did Alexander the Great have any connection to Luxor Temple?
faqs.answer: Yes, Alexander the Great added a granite chapel within Luxor Temple, depicting himself in traditional pharaonic style to legitimize his rule over Egypt.

faqs.question: Is Luxor Temple located inside the city?
faqs.answer: Yes, uniquely among major Egyptian monuments, Luxor Temple sits directly within the modern city center of Luxor, surrounded by streets, shops, and the Nile corniche.

faqs.question: Can I combine Luxor Temple and Karnak Temple in one visit?
faqs.answer: Yes, both temples are on the East Bank and relatively close together; many itineraries visit Karnak in the morning and Luxor Temple in the late afternoon or evening.

faqs.question: Is photography allowed at Luxor Temple?
faqs.answer: Yes, standard non-flash photography is generally permitted throughout the temple, including during evening floodlit visits.

faqs.question: Is Luxor Temple wheelchair accessible?
faqs.answer: It is one of the more accessible ancient sites in Luxor, with mostly flat, paved courtyards, though some interior areas retain uneven original stone flooring.

faqs.question: How far is Luxor Temple from the Valley of the Kings?
faqs.answer: The Valley of the Kings is on the West Bank of the Nile, roughly 15 km from Luxor Temple, and requires crossing the river by bridge or ferry, typically a 25–30 minute drive.
